newsitem.title: USA: U.S., in subtle shift on dollar, sends it down.
newsitem.headline: U.S., in subtle shift on dollar, sends it down.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin signalled Friday that he would not be unhappy with some weakening of the dollar, but he stopped well short of advocating a decline in the U.S. currency.
His comments, however, helped bring one about, driving the greenback sharply lower in the New York foreign exchange market as speculators scrambled to dump dollars.
A tireless advocate of a strong dollar, Rubin reiterated Friday that a strong U.S. currency was good for America.
But he also told reporters that the dollar has been strong for a while, indicating he would not stand in the way of some weakening of the greenback after its recent relentless rise.

"A strong dollar is in the U.S. interest," Rubin said ahead of a weekend meeting in Berlin of economic policymakers from the Group of Seven industrial nations. But he added, "We've had a strong dollar for some time."

His remarks, which seemed designed to subtly shift the market's perception of U.S. currency policy, helped push the dollar down by over two pfennigs against the German mark and by more than three yen against Japan's currency.
In late New York trading, the dollar finished at 1.6582 marks, up from late Thursday's 1.6535 reading. The dollar fell to 123 yen from 123.75 on Thursday.
Every time in the past that Rubin had spoken out in favour of a strong dollar, currency dealers read that as U.S. backing for an ever-stronger currency and acted accordingly.

But Rubin himself has been consistently careful to steer clear of saying he wanted a stronger dollar -- as opposed to a strong one -- and his remarks on Friday seemed designed to draw that to the market's attention.

He has to be careful though to avoid advocating a weak currency, because that could upset U.S. stock and bond markets. Bond prices did sag a bit on the dollar's weakness Friday, although they were still higher than Thursday.

Rubin said that he expects the foreign exchange market to be a "principal topic" of discussion at Saturday's meeting of economic policymakers from the G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
"Some G7 countries have expressed concern about the recent declines in their currencies," Rubin said. "We look forward to discussing these issues in Germany."

Japan has been the most vocal of those worried about the dollar's steep rise because of concern that could trigger a free-fall on the Tokyo stock market. Germany too has also shown some signs of uneasiness.
Since G7 policymakers last met in September, the dollar has risen nearly 10 percent against both the yen and mark.

Some U.S. companies, most notably automobile firms, have stepped up their complaints about the dollar as it has continued to rise. The strong dollar makes American producers less competitive on world markets, giving their foreign rivals an edge.
"The accelerating depreciation of the yen has gone from being a troubling trend to a serious problem," the big three U.S. automakers and their union said in an unusual joint statement Thursday.
As he has done before, Rubin said that ultimately, currency values reflect fundamentals.
Discussing those fundamentals, Rubin said that the U.S. economy was "performing well." But the prospects in Japan and continental Europe are "somewhat less clear," he said.
Growth in both continental Europe and Japan has lagged as the economies there have struggled to right themselves.

Rubin said that Japan needs to both maintain an economic policy mix that promotes strong domestic demand and avoid a renewed widening of its trade surplus. "You don't want them to backtrack," he said.

He refused, however, to prescribe a specific stance for Tokyo. Some analysts have voiced concern about Japan's plans to sharply tighten its budget policy, including raising its consumption tax, at a time when its economy is weak.
Rubin said the United States also has a "critical interest" in a strong and dynamic Europe.
Europe's head-long drive to reduce budget deficits as part of its effort to establish a single currency in 1999 has worried some analysts.
